about: The NPU's model server for each vendor, as data (NPU-VENDORS.md beside this file says why each was chosen and what is unverified): how detection tells the vendor and generation, the server's pinned download, how it installs, the models it pulls, its port, caps and timeouts. The node part's npu-vendors.ts reads it; setup installs from it. A server or model is changed here, with its pinned size and SHA-256, and released as a kit version. Sizes in bytes, times in milliseconds. %LOCALAPPDATA% and %USERPROFILE% are expanded; {tools} is the tools home (toolsHome), {port} the server's port, {model} a model's id.

idleStop.about: When the NPU's servers stop after a quiet spell (the keeper, keeper.ts), unless config.json's npuIdleStopMinutes says otherwise. The same rule stops a graphics card's llama.cpp servers on such a PC when the card shares the PC's memory (under 2 GB of its own: integrated graphics, whose models hold the PC's own memory), unless config.json's gpuIdleStopMinutes says otherwise, from cardColdStartMs: llama.cpp b11669's longest start from the disk cache to the first answer on an Intel Core Ultra 5 225U's graphics, 5.4 s for Qwen3-VL-4B with its projector (3.8 to 5.2 s for Qwen3-4B, 1.6 to 2.9 s for the embedding model), rounded up. A card with memory of its own keeps rules.json's keeper.gpuIdleStopMinutes. On a PC with less than smallPcGb of memory (Windows shows a 16 GB PC as 15.3 to 15.9; the next common size is 24 or 32), each route's own minutes per kind (its idleStop.minutes); on a bigger PC, rules.json's keeper.npuIdleStopMinutes, as before. A route's minutes are coldStartTimes times its cold start (idleStop.coldStartMs: stopped to the first answer), so waking it again costs at most a twentieth of the quiet spell it ends, and never under floorMinutes, so the pauses in a conversation, or between an agent's rounds, never pay it. None of the three servers can drop its model and keep running: GenieX's --keepalive unloads it, but the process keeps some 340 MB from every load until it exits; OpenVINO Model Server started with --source_model can't unload one (only its config-file mode can); FastFlowLM documents no unload. So the keeper stops the server, holding the NPU's turn, and the next request starts it again in its own turn.

meteor-lake.label: Core Ultra Series 1, 200U or 200H, Meteor Lake or Arrow Lake-U or -H (NPU 3720)
meteor-lake.basis: Measured by the NPU check on Intel Core Ultra 5 225U (Arrow Lake-U, whose NPU 3720 shows Meteor Lake's 7D1D), NPU driver 32.0.100.5540, 2026-10-14, every step passing, the prompt read 128 tokens at a time: writes 10.1 tokens a second: 200 ms a token allows twice that; reading 1550 tokens took 6.4 s: a 15 s base allows twice that and a warm answer. OpenVINO's own 1,024-token chunks cost every prompt a whole chunk: a short answer 3.1 s against 0.5, two at once 6.4 s against 1.2, 1,550 tokens 7.0 s against 4.0 to 6.4. Then 20 quick benchmarks on the same PC (npu-bench, 2026-10-14), each also reading prompts no cache had seen: in 64-token chunks a short answer took 0.35 s and 1,740 tokens 8.1 s; in 128, 0.5 s and 6.3 s; in 256, 0.78 s and 6.0 s; in 512, 1.43 s and 6.4 s; in 1,024, 3.1 s and 6.9 s: 128 stays. GENERATE_HINT BEST_PERF writes 12.3 to 13.1 tokens a second against 9.3 to 11.2, and the benchmark's jobs took 27.3 to 28.0 s against 29.1 to 35.6 (castellan-npu-bench/2, whose prompts no cache has seen, 2026-10-15), the same reads and answers; it doubles the first compile, 56.5 to 68.7 s against 25.8 to 28.9: the slowest start to a first answer took 69 s: 120 s allows half again. OpenVINO Model Server turns the NPU's prefix caching on: at the benchmark's end the server held 5.98 GB with its 128 blocks of 128 tokens, 4.30 GB with 32, and 3.72 GB with the cache off, which also read 2 to 5% faster and did the jobs in 27.25 to 27.48 s against 27.67 to 28.01 with 32 blocks (two runs each). The agents' prompts share 25 to 90 tokens at their start, less than a block, so a cache is hardly ever hit: the route's command turns it off (--enable_prefix_caching false: --plugin_config can't, OpenVINO Model Server refusing its key there as doubled), and 3.8 GB. PREFILL_HINT STATIC read every prompt in 7.4 s; NPU_TURBO was no faster, and STATIC prefill attention read 15 to 20% slower. A 3,072-token prompt held 0.4 GB more and read 5 to 10% slower; a 4,096-token one 1.0 GB more, past a 16 GB PC's room for chat and embeddings together. Its embeddings run on the processor's graphics (embedArgs), measured on the same PC's Intel Graphics, 2026-10-15, two runs each, the same model and command started by hand: a query in 49 to 50 ms against the NPU's 1.13 s, 16 of Reeve's chunks in 4.8 s against 18.0, a dense one (1,100 to 1,320 tokens) in 0.73 to 0.95 s against 2.5, the NPU's vectors (cosine 0.997 to 0.999), and 1.25 GB of the PC's memory against 1.14 to 1.18. Beside the chat server with this command, chat wrote 13.1 to 13.3 tokens a second while the graphics indexed, as alone, against 6.5 to 6.8 with both on the NPU. The NPU at --max_length 512 answered a query in 0.27 s but refused Reeve's dense chunks; the processor slowed chat by a fifth and took 2.3 GB.

arrow-lake.label: Core Ultra 200S or 200HX, Arrow Lake-S or -HX (NPU 3720)

lunar-lake.label: Core Ultra 200V, Lunar Lake (NPU 4)
lunar-lake.basis: Measured by the NPU check on a Lunar Lake (Core Ultra 7 256V), 2026-10-12, with OpenVINO's own prompt settings and prefix cache: the route's timeouts, cap and memory. Its prompt settings are estimated from the NPU 3720 (meteor-lake), the only other Intel NPU there is to run (NPU-VENDORS.md, Estimated): the NPU 4 read a 1,024-token chunk in 0.23 to 0.26 of the NPU 3720's time, and a chunk costs a fixed part and a part for each of its tokens. In 512-token chunks a short prompt should take 0.3 to 0.4 s, what the NPU 3720 takes in its 128, against 0.72 s in OpenVINO's 1,024, and the jobs' prompts 18 to 27% less, whether or not the fixed part is faster on the NPU 4. The NPU 3720 at this 4,096-token prompt bears it out: in 512-token chunks it read about 3,500 tokens in 12.9 to 13.3 s, against 15.0 to 15.8 in 128 and 16.2 to 16.6 in 1,024. GENERATE_HINT BEST_PERF wrote 30% faster there for about twice the first compile (80 to 90 s against 42): 31 to 41 s here, so about 60 to 90 s, inside the 180 s cold load. The prefix cache is off, as on every Intel NPU (the route's command, meteor-lake): the agents' prompts share too little to hit it, and at 4,096 tokens on the NPU 3720 it held 0.4 to 0.6 GB more, read no faster, and at OpenVINO's default 128 blocks grew to 6.17 GB.

idleStop.basis: The slowest measured, rounded up to a tenth of a second: npu-check --idle on the NPU 3720 (Core Ultra 5 225U, 2026-10-15), every step passing, its servers stopped by the keeper after a minute unused and woken by a person's request: chat started to its first answer in 6.85 s, embeddings in 2.74 s, from the compile cache (--cache_dir). On a Lunar Lake chat started in 4 s (2026-10-12), and its embeddings weren't timed apart. The first compile (31 to 41 s there, about a minute on an NPU 3720 with BEST_PERF) is once per PC and model, not per start. 20 times either cold start is under 5 minutes, so 5.
idleStop.verify: Run on the NPU 3720 (2026-10-15); still to run on a Lunar Lake laptop with 16 GB (Windows shows 15.3 to 15.9), with OpenVINO Model Server set up by setup: stop the manor's own NPU servers first (or let the keeper stop them), then run node <agent>\src\kit\npu-check.ts --idle --yes from any agent that has the kit (2.71.0 or later). It starts the chat and embedding servers through the kit, has the keeper stop both once the NPU has been unused a minute (idle-stop: their processes gone, the memory freed said), asks again as a person would with a 20 s timeout (idle-cold-answer: told the local AI is waking, answered within the cold load; the time is this PC's cold start), and checks a request in flight is never stopped (idle-in-flight). It passes or fails each step and prints the idleStop numbers its cold start gives; if they differ from these, change coldStartMs and minutes here.

intel.embeddings: on the NPU, through a second OpenVINO Model Server of its own (one process serves one task from the command line): OpenVINO's channel-wise INT4 Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, last-token pooling, compiled for 2,048 tokens. The NPU compiles a fixed shape, so every request costs the full 2,048 and a longer one is refused (400); a dense 1,500-character chunk (UUIDs, hex, base64) is up to 1,338 tokens, so 1,024 wouldn't do. Its cap, 680 by the kit's estimate of 3 characters a token, keeps a request under 2,048 real tokens at nearly one a character. Measured on a Lunar Lake 2026-10-13: the graphics card's own results (OpenVINO, the same model), a query in 166 ms and 16 of Reeve's chunks in 2.6 s, against 5.9 s on the Arc through llama.cpp's Vulkan build, which setup gives the card

model.licence: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B: Apache-2.0 (OpenVINO's channel-wise INT4 export of it)

intel.vision: none on the NPU yet: OpenVINO's Qwen3-VL-4B INT4 build is asymmetric, which the NPU doesn't take, and OpenVINO Model Server 2026.4.1 fails its prompt on the NPU (prompt_ids.get_size() >= tokenized_history.size(), a Lunar Lake 2026-10-13) while answering on the graphics card; vision goes to the graphics card or the processor
intel.notes: A zip, unpacked into the tools home: no installer, no administrator. Its programs need the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime, which its zip doesn't carry (only its Python's vcruntime140): setup copies the five DLLs they import from Microsoft's own CRT package (runtime, pinned) beside ovms.exe, where Windows loads them first, so no administrator installs the Redistributable (run on a Lunar Lake, 2026-10-12). It needs Intel's NPU driver 32.0.100.4023 or later. It serves the OpenAI routes at /v1 (and the older /v3), source-checked at v2026.4.1. The NPU compiles a model on first load (minutes), cached in --cache_dir. Its zip wraps everything in an ovms folder, which setup unpacks into ovms-2026.4.1; its Python (for chat templates) needs PYTHONHOME and PATH, which the entry's env gives (its setupvars script does the same). Its model is a channel-wise INT4 export (symmetric, one scale per output channel), the kind the NPU runs properly: the group-wise AWQ export it had first, OpenVINO's Qwen3-4B-int4-ov, loads and answers fast on a Lunar Lake NPU, but nonsense ("?option?option…"), while answering properly on the same PC's processor and graphics card (2026-10-12). OpenVINO publishes channel-wise exports of other models (Qwen3-8B-int4-cw-ov, 4.7 GB, also answered properly there, at 14.8 tokens a second) but none of a Qwen3 4B, so Castellan made one of Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (optimum-cli export openvino --weight-format int4 --sym --ratio 1.0 --group-size -1; its model card has the versions) and publishes it as Castellan-AI/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-int4-cw-ov, its files pinned for every generation (OpenVINO's model is the same file on each: each PC compiles it for its own NPU). The NPU check with it on that Lunar Lake (Core Ultra 7 256V, NPU driver 32.0.100.4512, 2026-10-12), every step passed: the first load with its compile 31 s, from its cache 4 s; 26 tokens written and about 670 read a second; a short answer warm in 0.7 s; 1,395 tokens answered and 1,792 refused plainly (400) at --max_prompt_len 1536, the server still up; two requests at once both answered; 3.6 GB working set. Its cap is now 4,096 (--max_prompt_len 4096; the check again, 2026-10-13, every step passed): the first load 41 s; a short answer warm in 0.8 s, 24 to 28 tokens written a second; 3,112 tokens read in 4.6 s; 3,827 answered and 4,352 refused plainly (400), the server still up; 4.3 GB working set. The bigger compile costs a short prompt about 70 ms (a short answer 799 ms against 715, 512 tokens read in 830 ms against 761) and the benchmark's jobs nothing (11.0 s against 11.8). The timeouts leave room for Meteor Lake's slower NPU 3720, not yet measured (the check suggested base 15 s, 100 ms a token, cold load 90 s on Lunar Lake). Its embedding server beside it (embedServer) adds 1.7 GB; the two run on the NPU at once.

xdna2.label: Ryzen AI 300 and later: Strix Point, Krackan, Strix Halo, Gorgon Point (XDNA 2)
xdna2.basis: Measured by the NPU check on AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 w/ Radeon 860M (Krackan, 16 GB), NPU driver 32.0.20102.3930, 2026-10-15, Qwen3.5-2B for chat and vision, its context 4,096 (--ctx-len), every measuring step passing: writes 19.4 tokens a second: 150 ms a token allows twice that; reading 3,272 tokens took 4.1 s: a 15 s base allows twice that and a warm answer; the slowest start to a first answer took 17 s (the kit's test request, a picture and then chat): 30 s allows half again. One model answers chat and pictures, so nothing switches between them. Qwen3-4B's, before it: writes 13.8 tokens a second, 3,115 tokens read in 6.6 s, a 20 s base, and its switch to and from its vision model, 8 to 9 s, inside each.

powerTool.broken: an older AMD NPU driver left its files in Windows\System32\AMD, where AMD's xrt-smi.exe loads them and can't start, and FastFlowLM sets the power mode with xrt-smi. Removing that older driver package fixes it (an administrator's job, with pnputil /delete-driver)

idleStop.basis: The slowest measured, rounded up to a tenth of a second, Qwen3.5-2B for chat and vision. Chat: npu-check --idle on a Ryzen AI 7 350 (Krackan, 16 GB), 2026-10-15, every step passing: stopped to its first answer in 15.0 s (FastFlowLM loads the model before it opens its port), the keeper's stop freeing 3.7 GB. Vision: the NPU check's kit-test the same day, the kit's test request on a stopped server, a picture and then chat, 16.5 s: the same server and model, so no switch. Started alike from Node, three times each, Qwen3.5-2B answered first in 11.8 to 12.4 s and Qwen3-4B in 10.1 to 10.7 s; Qwen3-4B's idleStop was 6.6 s for chat and 15.7 s for vision (its switch to the vision model, 9.2 s, included). All of these were measured while Reeve embedded on the Radeon 860M, which shares the PC's memory with the NPU: Qwen3-4B's server came up in 8.5 to 9.3 s then, against 4 to 6 s on the quiet PC that gave its 6.6 s, so they are on the slow side.
idleStop.verify: On a Ryzen AI 300 (XDNA 2) laptop with 16 GB, with FastFlowLM set up by setup: stop the manor's own NPU server first (or let the keeper stop it), then run node <agent>\src\kit\npu-check.ts --idle --yes from any agent that has the kit (2.71.0 or later). It passes or fails each step and prints the idleStop numbers its cold start gives; if they differ from these, change coldStartMs and minutes here.

offNpu.basis: Qwen3.5-2B, the model FastFlowLM runs on the NPU, as unsloth's Q4_0 GGUF and F16 projector (Hugging Face, unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF at f6d5376b, Apache-2.0), run by llama.cpp b11734 on the Radeon (its Vulkan build) and on the processor (its x64 build), at FastFlowLM's --ctx-len 4096 and with its thinking off, as FastFlowLM serves it. FastFlowLM's own weights are in its NPU format (q4nx), which nothing else reads: Q4_0 is the nearest 4-bit GGUF. Downloaded into the tools home's models folder (1.9 GB), for the benchmark only.

amd.notes: A portable zip, unpacked into the tools home: no installer, no administrator. AMD's NPU driver 32.0.203.311 or later (an administrator installs drivers). One server holds one model: Qwen3.5-2B answers chat and pictures alike, so nothing switches (the Qwen3-4B pair before it, one model for chat and one for vision, took 8 to 9 s to switch either way). Models are kept in %USERPROFILE%\.flm\models. Its context is --ctx-len 4096, the cap: FastFlowLM holds its whole context on the NPU from the start, and without it took the model's own, 40,960 tokens for Qwen3-4B (about 144 KB a token, 5.6 GB, on top of 3.3 GB of weights). On a Ryzen AI 7 350 with 16 GB, where Windows lets a device hold half the PC's memory at once (7.6 GB), that never loaded (XRT 0xc01e0200, the video memory manager couldn't page every allocation in at once), from a fresh start too; at 4,096 Qwen3-4B loaded in 4 to 6 s and held 4.5 GB, at 8,192 10.6 s and 5.1 GB, at the same speed (13.9 to 14.1 tokens a second), and its vision model held 5.3 GB. Qwen3.5-2B at 4,096 holds 3.7 GB started and 4.0 to 4.1 GB after jobs and pictures, writes 19.4 to 21.0 tokens a second and reads about 800. Its tokenizer has 248,320 entries against Qwen3's 151,936, so the same text is usually fewer tokens to it, and the kit's estimate of 3 characters a token stays on the safe side. FastFlowLM serves it with its thinking off. A failed load doesn't stop it: it serves on, /v1/models listing every model it knows, and answers each request 200 with only {"error":"Failed to load … model!"} (it tries the load again each time); the kit takes that for the server failing (failedWithOk), and the NPU check asks /api/ps, which lists the model it holds (reportsLoaded). A prompt past its context is refused 400 ("Max length reached!"), the server still up. Its power mode: at each start FastFlowLM runs C:\Windows\System32\AMD\xrt-smi.exe configure --pmode (performance by default) and ignores the result. On the Krackan that never ran: an older driver's xrt_coreutil.dll (2024) beside the newer xrt-smi.exe lacks a function it needs, so xrt-smi failed to load at every start (silently from Node, which the kit starts it from; with a dialog for each start from anywhere else). So its --pmode runs (powersaver, balanced, performance, turbo: the same speed on mains power, 14.0 tokens a second each, and on battery, none drawing clearly less than the battery meter's own swing) all ran in one mode, the driver's own, and say nothing of the modes: the route sets none until they're measured on a PC whose xrt-smi runs. With Qwen3-4B, in that one mode, on battery it used 20.7 mJ a token (npu-bench --energy), wrote 13.1 tokens a second and loaded in 12.7 s (5.4 s on mains power), and a smaller --prefill-chunk-len than its 4,096 only read slower (3,000 tokens 7.3 s at 1,024, 9.5 s at 512, against 5.3 s). It reads far faster than it writes: Qwen3-4B 34 to 36 times (472 to 512 tokens a second read, 13.1 to 14.4 written, on mains power and on battery), Qwen3.5-2B 41 times (795 and 19.4), so readPerWrite is 30: on a generation nobody has measured, calibrate takes a full-cap read at 30 times the writing speed it measured (the Krackan's --harden measurement gave a 35 s base with Qwen3-4B and 25 s with Qwen3.5-2B, where the kit's 10 gave 90 s). Its --img-pre-resize default (2: a large picture scaled to a height of 720; a small one isn't enlarged) is kept, measured with Qwen3-4B's vision model: a 1920x1080 screen cost 960 tokens and 4.5 s an answer and a 1080x2400 phone screen 270 tokens and 2.3 s, every answer right, where the original size cost 2,080 and 2,600 tokens and twice to four times the time for nothing more right, and a height of 480 misread small text. FastFlowLM 1.0.7 misreads a picture it doesn't shrink (720 px tall or less) when a side is a whole number of 32 px, so the route has the quirk sides-of-32: the kit makes such a side a pixel longer before sending it (NPU-VENDORS.md, FastFlowLM's pictures with sides of 32 px). It keeps no prefix cache: a request asked again costs the same. It streams a token a chunk, with its usage in the last (stream_options.include_usage).
